title: Listening Diagnostic Test 3 - Set 2 (Cam 21 Test 2: Part 3 & Part 4)

parts.title: Part 3: Food Science Course Feedback
parts.transcriptHtml:
14:25ANNOUNCER: You will hear two food science students called Nadia and Fergus talking to their tutor about their course.
14:34ANNOUNCER: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
15:10ANNOUNCER: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
15:18TUTOR: Thanks for coming along Nadia and Fergus, so this is a chance for you to give us some feedback about different aspects of your course. What would you like to begin with?
15:30NADIA: I've enjoyed the sessions on food safety. There was some information there that I found really surprising, although some was stuff I knew already, like the rise in rates of obesity.
15:41FERGUS: Yeah, that's been in the news a lot.
15:43NADIA: But I hadn't realised that unsafe food causes more than 200 different diseases.
15:49FERGUS: No. I had no idea it was that many. And speaking of diseases, I knew resistance to antibiotics is on the increase, but I didn't know why. That it's partly because when animals are treated with antibiotics then consumed by humans, the antibiotics get into the food chain.
16:09NADIA: I had no idea about that either. Hmm.
16:12FERGUS: Then the sessions provided a lot of information about plastic pollution from food packaging in the ocean. But I think that most of us were already aware of that.
16:22NADIA: Yeah, but I thought we could have done more on how much food is thrown away unnecessarily through fear of it being out of date. That was only mentioned in passing.
16:32TUTOR: OK, I'll bear that in mind. What did you think about the sessions from visiting lecturers? Fergus?
16:39FERGUS: For me, the most interesting one was about that project to prevent companies giving incorrect information to consumers about food.
16:47TUTOR: Ah, food fraud, yes.
16:50FERGUS: I thought it was really good to address a problem that's faced by so many different groups. People with special religious rules, as well as vegetarians and vegans, and those with allergies.
17:01NADIA: Yeah. And another thing, we've had effective ways of analysing DNA for some time now, and these can easily be applied to analysing food. But what the researchers succeeded in doing was to ensure that these tests were carried out at different stages in the food's journey, from the producer to the consumer. So they knew that the food actually came from the place it was supposed to and had the ingredients it was meant to.
17:27TUTOR: Exactly. So customers can be confident about what they buy.
17:32FERGUS: And the researchers had a good system for publicising their findings too.
17:36NADIA: Well, I thought there were some problems with that actually.
17:40TUTOR: OK. And do you have any recommendations for new topics that we could include in the course?
17:47FERGUS: Well, I'm interested in how crop yields can be increased without damaging the environment. But we've already done quite a bit on that. But not so much on the seafood industry, where stocks are in danger of being over-exploited as a food source, unless we can find ways of keeping stocks up.
18:04TUTOR: Yes. That'd be a good topic.
18:07NADIA: And I'm interested in the idea of a personalised approach to diet. Now we have the technology to analyse exactly what individuals need.
18:17TUTOR: That sounds more like a medical topic than food science.
18:20NADIA: OK.
18:22FERGUS: What about sessions on the variety of food and eating habits around the world? That's very relevant nowadays.
18:29NADIA: Yes, I think the whole class would be interested in that.
18:32FERGUS: Then there's technological stuff, things like 3D printing of food and smart packaging.
18:38TUTOR: Hmm, maybe too specialist.
18:44ANNOUNCER: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
19:09ANNOUNCER: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
19:17TUTOR: Now I'm particularly interested in your project, the one where you developed a new food product. So talk me through the stages. First you had to decide on your initial aim.
19:30FERGUS: We decided we wanted to create something people could eat on the go rather than in a restaurant.
19:36NADIA: Yeah, so we chose Falafel, which was originally a Middle Eastern snack. We made up our minds about that pretty quickly. I know some students found this a lot harder to choose and wasted a lot of time.
19:49FERGUS: Then we had to do the literature review. We hadn't done one of these before, so the handout with advice for the project was very useful here.
19:58NADIA: Yes, especially the advice on how to present the information.
20:03FERGUS: Then, product development, actually deciding what we'd use to make the falafel. And for me, the interesting thing about that was that we wanted it to be something a bit different from an ordinary falafel. We really made the right choice when we finally decided to use jackfruit, even though it wasn't something that either of us had ever tasted before.
20:26NADIA: Yeah, like the name tells you, it's a fruit but actually it's really good in savoury dishes.
20:33FERGUS: The product production, working out how to make the falafel, was harder than I expected because I'd never made them before. It was mostly trial and error. We started off with the basic recipe, and then experimented, and when it went wrong...
20:50NADIA: Which it did a lot of the time.
20:53FERGUS: We just moved on and kept adapting it. And in the end, it turned out fine. And we had a lot of fun.
21:00NADIA: We did. Thank you.

groups.title: Questions 27–30
groups.instructions:
What comment do the students make about each of the following stages in developing their new food product?
Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to Questions 27–30.

options.text: It required frequent experimentation to get right.
They made their decision faster than other students.
They found the written advice especially helpful.
They were glad they selected an unfamiliar ingredient.
It proved to be cheaper than expected.
It was difficult to agree on an initial plan.

q21.text: What surprised both Nadia and Fergus during the sessions on food safety?
options: A. The wide variety of illnesses that unsafe food can trigger.
B. The rapid increase in obesity levels among populations.
C. The extent of plastic pollution caused by food packaging.

steps: • Dấu hiệu: 'unsafe food causes more than 200 different diseases... I had no idea it was that many'

q22.text: What did Fergus learn regarding the issue of antibiotic resistance?
options: A. Patients are taking larger doses of medication than required.
B. Farm livestock pass antibiotics into the human food supply.
C. Most antibiotics used today are completely ineffective.

steps: • Dấu hiệu: 'when animals are treated with antibiotics then consumed by humans, the antibiotics get into the food chain'

q23.text: What aspect of food safety did Nadia feel was not covered sufficiently?
options: A. The contamination of marine environments by plastics.
B. Unnecessary food wastage caused by expiration dates.
C. The health hazards of consuming processed meat.

steps: • Dấu hiệu: 'how much food is thrown away unnecessarily through fear of it being out of date. That was only mentioned in passing'

q24.text: What did Fergus find most positive about the visiting lecture on food fraud?
options: A. It dealt with an issue that affects various consumer groups.
B. It introduced a quick method for exposing dishonest sellers.
C. It highlighted cooperation between government authorities.

steps: • Dấu hiệu: 'address a problem that's faced by so many different groups'

q25.text: According to Nadia, what was the major breakthrough of the food fraud project?
options: A. Developing a cheaper and faster procedure for DNA sequencing.
B. Carrying out verification tests at various stages of the supply chain.
C. Creating a public database to verify origin labels.

steps: • Dấu hiệu: 'tests were carried out at different stages in the food's journey, from the producer to the consumer'

q26.text: Which potential new topic was approved by both the tutor and the students?
options: A. Sustainable practices in the seafood sector.
C. Industrial applications of 3D food printing.

parts.title: Part 4: Tourism Presentation on the Cruise Ship Industry
parts.transcriptHtml:
21:44ANNOUNCER: You will hear part of a presentation by a Tourism Studies student on the cruise ship industry.
21:53ANNOUNCER: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
22:49ANNOUNCER: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
22:57SPEAKER: For my presentation today I'm going to talk about some of the issues facing the cruise ship industry and then some ways these can be addressed. The cruise ship industry has partly been responsible for the effects of overtourism in recent decades. Overtourism occurs in places where excessive numbers of tourists cause significant problems. Pollution, for example, is among the greatest threats to many popular tourist destinations.
23:27SPEAKER: Of course, for many places, it's a difficult balance to achieve. They want to promote their city or island as a desirable tourist destination, but at the same time are unable to cope with thousands of cruise ship passengers on a daily basis. The trouble is, excessive tourism is destroying the beauty spots and places of interest that people come to visit.
23:52SPEAKER: Several cities, such as Barcelona, have responded by imposing a tax, which all visitors to the city from cruise ships have to pay. But as it's only a couple of euros, many green campaigners think it won't deter enough people to make any difference.
24:10SPEAKER: Bruges is another city which became impossible to navigate at times because of the huge numbers of cruise passengers arriving on day trips from the port of Zeebrugge. The city was becoming like a theme park with shops only catering for tourists selling chocolate, which Belgium is famous for, and other souvenirs. The local council took action to limit cruise passengers to a more manageable level.
24:39SPEAKER: Dubrovnik had to limit the numbers of cruise ships after it became extremely popular as a cruise ship destination when it featured in a hugely successful TV series. What it does now is control the timing of all cruise ship entries to the city's port. However, many people feel this measure does not go far enough.
25:05SPEAKER: Cruise ships may be unpopular in some of their destinations, but they also have an image problem. They've always been perceived as a safe holiday for the elderly, with not much on offer for families or young couples. A recent survey showed that cost is also a major factor in putting younger groups off going on a cruise. But what they don't realize is that compared to other types of package holidays, cruises can actually be good value, as all activities and drinks are often included.
25:39SPEAKER: And another perception is that cruises have lots of rules about what to wear and how to behave. But these days, most cruises are no longer very formal and behind the times.
25:52SPEAKER: So what solutions are there for cruise lines to overcome some of these problems? How can they appeal to younger customers? Well, one selling point is that cruise ships are becoming more sustainable. New ships are built with hybrid engines with large batteries, which means ships do not have to keep their engines running while docked.
26:15SPEAKER: Cruise lines are also designing ships, especially for those in the age range of 21 to 45. The decor in these feels contemporary, and there are a range of activities on board that you wouldn't find on a more traditional cruise. There's even a boxing ring on one ship, and most offer diving expeditions. But there's also a huge focus on well-being, with a variety of sessions of different kinds.
26:44SPEAKER: Food is always a very important part of any cruise, and cruise ships have had to radically update their menus to suit the tastes of their younger customers. Vegan dishes are standard, for example. The restaurants on board have also gone paperless, with menus available on screen.
27:05SPEAKER: Unlike older generations who went on cruises largely to get away from everything, younger people expect to be able to keep in touch with friends and family. Many people going on longer cruises also spend time working, so companies have to guarantee Wi-Fi that can be relied upon at all times.
27:25SPEAKER: My grandparents used to love looking through cruise brochures, even when they weren't planning on going on a cruise. Until very recently, TV ads for cruises always felt dated and aimed at retirees. Cruise lines have been slow to adopt the power of social media, but that's all changing. Leading cruise lines now employ top agencies to produce first-rate videos for social media channels.
